Stiff-Man Syndrome
Report of a Case
Daniel Tarsy, MD, Edison K. Miyawaki, MD
Stiff-man
syndrome is a well-described, but rare and often overlooked, neuromuscular
syndrome of rigidity, spasm, and gait abnormality that is associated with several en-
docrinologic and autoimmune disorders. A patient exhibiting many typical features
of stiff-man syndrome had intermittent symptoms for 22 years before the correct di-
agnosis was made. Similar to many described patients, she was diabetic, hyperthyroid, and had
elevated islet cell, antithyroid, and glutamic acid decarboxylase antibody levels. The high fre-
quency of diabetes mellitus among patients with stiff-man syndrome is emphasized, as is in-
creasing evidence to suggest that elaboration of anti\p=m-\glutamic acid decarboxylase and anti\p=m-\islet
cell antibodies may play a role in the pathophysiologic state of the disorder.
(Arch Intern Med. 1994;154:1285-1288)
Stiff-man syndrome (SMS) is a rare neu¬
rologic disorder of unknown cause
characterized by progressive and fluctu¬
ating axial muscular rigidity, painful
muscle spasms, and abnormal gait. An
association with diabetes mellitus has
long been recognized,1 and in a recent
review, 20 of 84 patients with SMS were
found to have diabetes mellitus.2
Moersch and Woltman1 first described
14 patients with this distinctive clinical
syndrome who were seen at the Mayo
Clinic, Rochester, Minn, over a 32-year
period. No specific laboratory or elec-
trophysiologic abnormalities were de¬
scribed, although four patients had "re¬
ducing substances" in the urine. Since
their report, several reviews have been
published and criteria have been estab¬
lished for the diagnosis of SMS.3"6 Be¬
cause of the extreme rarity of this disor¬
der, its highly unusual and sometimes
bizarre symptoms, absence of abnormal
neurologic findings, lack of specific
laboratory abnormalities, and frequent
association with psychological abnor-
malities, patients' conditions usually re¬
main undiagnosed for prolonged peri¬
ods, and many patients are mistakenly
thought to suffer from a hysterical psy¬
chiatric disorder. The patient presented
in this report was symptomatic for 22
years before the diagnosis was made.
REPORT OF A CASE
A 54-year-old woman presented in 1986
with a 17-year history of intermittent,
painless extensor spasms of both legs.
Insulin-dependent diabetes began in
1968 and she was treated with a combi¬
nation of isophane insulin suspension
(NPH insulin) and regular human insu¬
lin. Multinodular goiter with intermit¬
tent hyperthyroidism had been diag¬
nosed and the patient was treated with
radioactive iodine 131 in 1982. Exami¬
nation in 1986 disclosed anxiety, left leg
stiffness, exaggerated lumbar lordosis,
and a hesitant gait. Brain magnetic reso¬
nance imaging, cervical myelography,
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination,
and thyroid function test results were
normal. She was placed on a regimen of

diazepam for management of
anxiety with gradual improvement
in gait over several weeks. She re¬
mained relatively asymptomatic
until 1990 when identical symp¬
toms reappeared. Anxiety was
again prominent, and she was
treated with buspirone hydrochlo-
ride; this was followed by in¬
creased symptoms. In 1991, inter¬
mittent spasms of the legs, lower
part of the trunk, and left shoul¬
der appeared that were once again
attributed to anxiety. Spasms were
precipitated by movements of the
legs in bed and attempts to walk,
resulting in frequent sudden falls.
At the time of hospital admis¬
sion, she was extremely anxious and
unwilling to leave her bed because
of fear of precipitating spasms. Ex¬
tensor spasms and tremor appeared
in both legs with any attempt to arise
from bed and following rectal ex¬
amination. Painful spasms lasted for
30 to 60 seconds and were associ¬
ated with fear and anxiety. There was
lumbar hyperlordosis with marked
hypertrophy of the paralumbar
muscles. While the patient was in a
supine position, rigidity was absent
but the hyperlordotic posture per¬
sisted. There was no muscle weak¬
ness or atrophy. Sensation was nor¬
mal. Electromyography showed
continuous firing of motor units in
paralumbar muscles with the pa¬
tient at rest. Thyroid function stud¬
ies indicated hyperthyroidism, in¬
cluding the following values:
triiodothyronine, 3.6 nmol/L (234
ng/dL) (reference range, 1.5 to 2.9
nmol/L [100 to 190 ng/dL]); thy-
roxine, 216 nmol/L (reference range,
58 to 148 nmol/L); thyrotropin, 0.08
mU/L (reference range, 0.15 to 3.2
mU/L); and free thyroxine, 9 pmol/L
(reference range, 9 to 23 pmol/L).
Thyroid isotope scan showed evi¬
dence for toxic multinodular goi¬
ter. Islet cell antibody levels were el¬
evated at 1:640 JDF units, thyroid
microsomal antibody levels were el¬
evated at 1:1600, and antibody titer
against glutamic acid decarboxy¬
lase (GAD) was strongly positive.
Thyroglobulin and antiparietal cell
antibodies were absent. HLA typ¬
ing was as follows: DR3;
DQA1*0501; DQB1*0201; and
DRB1*0301 homozygous. She was
treated with diazepam, 20 mg daily,
with prompt reduction in the fre¬
quency of spasms and an increased
ability to stand and ambulate nor¬
mally. Hyperthyroidism was treated
with radioactive iodine 131. Dur¬
ing follow-up over the next 24
months increased doses of diaz¬
epam to 60 mg daily have contin¬
ued to suppress muscle spasm.
Although the clinical picture pre¬
sented by this patient is typical of
SMS, she was symptomatic for 22
years before a correct diagnosis was
made. The anxiety-related exacer¬
bations, axial muscular rigidity, lum¬
bar hyperlordosis, painful muscle
spasms precipitated by attempts to
walk, electromyographic pattern of
continuous involuntary firing of mo¬
tor units at rest, and prompt re¬
sponse to treatment with diazepam
all fulfilled the clinical criteria for di¬
agnosis of this disorder.3"6 The
presence of hyperthyroidism, dia¬
betes mellitus, elevated islet cell
antibodies, thyroid microsomal
antibodies, and antibodies against
GAD provided additional convinc¬
ing laboratory evidence for the di¬
agnosis of SMS.
Stiff-man syndrome typically
begins insidiously with stiffness of
lower back muscles followed by
painful spasms, precipitation of
symptoms by environmental stimuli
or emotional upsets, stiff and awk¬
ward gait due to axial rigidity, fear
of spasms, and sudden falls.3"5'7Hy¬
pertrophy of paraspinal lumbar
muscles with hyperlordosis is often

a characteristic physical sign, but re¬
sults of neurologic examination are
otherwise normal. In severe cases,
extreme muscle rigidity may pro¬
duce joint deformities, muscle tears,
bone fractures, and interference with
respiration.7
Neurologie disorders that re¬
semble SMS include certain rare
spasmodic muscle disorders char¬
acterized by continuous motor
unit activity, such as acute or
chronic tetanus,8 the syndrome of
continuous muscle fiber activity
associated with hyperhidrosis,9
painful rigidity and spasms rarely
associated with adrenal insuffi¬
ciency,7 and rare forms of viral en-
cephalomyelitis of the brain stem
and spinal cord associated with
muscle spasm and rigidity.10 On
the other hand, basal ganglia dis¬
orders that cause axial dystonia
and rigidity such as torsion dysto¬
nia, progressive supranuclear
palsy, Wilson's disease, and some
parkinsonian syndromes all pro¬
duce other distinctive central ner¬
vous system signs that serve to
distinguish them from SMS.
Electromyography shows per¬
sistent motor unit activity with in¬
complete muscle relaxation at rest
without other demonstrable abnor¬
malities of nerve, muscle, or neuro-
muscular junction. Bursts of elec-
tromyographic activity may occur in
response to somatosensory and
acoustic stimuli.1112 Treatment
with benzodiazepines such as di-
azepam13 or clonazepam14 is re¬
markably effective, although un¬
usually high doses are often
required. Valproate sodium and
baclofen have also been helpful in
individual patients.14"16
THE
NEUROPHYSI-
OLOG1C basis for this
disorder is obscure.
There is no clinical,
electromyographic,
or pathologic evidence for primary
muscle disease. Olafson et al1' pro¬
posed that impaired Renshaw cell
function caused loss of inhibition of
motor neurons. Gordon et al3 sug¬
gested that increased activity in y-ef-
ferent innervation of muscle spindles
was responsible. More recent theo¬
ries have implicated brain-stem
dysfunction with loss of supraseg-

mental inhibition of spinal motor
neurons supplying axial and limb
musculature.4
Recent evidence suggests that
SMS may be an autoimmune disor¬
der.27 Young18 reported two cases of
SMS associated with pernicious ane¬
mia and Hashimoto's thyroiditis. In
a recent review,213 (15%) of 84 pa¬
tients with SMS had clinical evi¬
dence for other autoimmune disor¬
ders, including Hashimoto's
thyroiditis, Graves' disease, perni¬
cious anemia, vitiligo, and myasthe-
nia gravis. Several patients with SMS
have been found to have elevated lev¬
els of IgG in the CSF.1920 Associa¬
tions with several endocrine disor¬
ders have also emerged, including
diabetes mellitus,1'2'13'21 hyperthy-
roidism,4,22'23 hypothyroidism,24 and
hypopituitarism.25 Of these, the as¬
sociation with diabetes mellitus is the
strongest. The original report by
Moersch and Woltman1 stated that
four patients had a reducing sub¬
stance in the urine, although three
of these patients had normal fasting
blood glucose levels. Overall, seven
(8%) of 84 patients with SMS re¬
cently reviewed by Blum and
Jankovic2 had insulin-dependent
diabetes mellitus (IDDM), a fre¬
quency over 30 times that in the
general population. Thirteen other
patients had diabetes mellitus,
type not specified.
Solimena et al20 reported the
presence of antibodies against
GAD, the enzyme responsible for
the synthesis of y-aminobutyric
acid (GABA) in the serum and
CSF of a patient with SMS who
also had IDDM. They subse¬
quently reported antibodies
against GAD in 24 of 33 serum
specimens from patients with SMS
sent to the laboratory from vari¬
ous centers worldwide.21 Both se¬
rum and CSF produced intense
and specific immunostaining of
rat and human neuronal perikarya
and dendrites in a distribution
corresponding with GABA-ergic
terminals.2021 Other investigators
have subsequently confirmed the
finding of autoantibodies to
GABA-containing neurons in pa¬
tients with SMS.212-26"28 The possi¬
bility that autoantibodies against
GABA-ergic neurons produce
muscle spasm by disinhibition of
spinal cord motor neurons is an
intriguing possibility, but it is un¬
proved at the present time. As
pointed out by Solimena et al,21
GAD is thought to be an intracel-
lular antigen and therefore may
not be directly exposed to the im¬
mune system.
A
HIGH INCIDENCE of
organ-specific an¬
tibodies has been
found in patients
with SMS, includ¬
ing gastric-parietal cell antibodies,
thyroid microsomal-fraction anti¬
bodies, and thyroglobulin anti¬
bodies.21 Autoantibodies to GAD
are said to be the earliest and most
predictive autoantibody marker
for IDDM.28'29 Because GAD is
highly concentrated in pancreatic
beta cells,21 islet cell antibodies
are found in virtually all patients
with SMS who have GAD autoan¬
tibodies.621'28 Although patients
with IDDM without SMS may also
have islet cell antibodies, the
staining pattern is different from
patients with SMS, and titers are
usually much lower.6 The fact that
only a very small percentage of
patients with IDDM and GAD au¬
toantibodies have development of
SMS suggests that additional fac¬
tors are required for the appear¬
ance of SMS, such as a stronger
antibody response to GAD and ad¬
ditional epitope recognition of
GABA-secreting neurons usually
absent in patients with IDDM.28
As indicated by Blum and Jan-
kovic,2 the relationship between
IDDM and SMS may not be coin¬
cidental. The configuration of
HLA-determined immunoregula-
tory molecules involved in
IDDM30 may alter the immune

system to allow for autoimmunity
to GABA-ergic cells in the central
nervous system. HLA-DR3 and
HLA-DR4 phenotypes, most com¬
monly associated with IDDM in
whites, were also present in three
patients with SMS in whom the
antigen was typed.2 HLA typing in
our patient identified the
DQB 1*0201 alíele, similar to 13 of
18 patients with SMS recently de¬
scribed by Pugliese et al.31
Because SMS may be an auto¬
immune disorder, treatment with
plasmapheresis and immunosup-
pression has been attempted with
mixed results. In published re¬
ports, plasmapheresis has been ef¬
fective in two patients1232but not in
six others.262733 If GAD autoanti-
body is synthesized intrathecally,
plasmapheresis might not be ex¬
pected to help.2,27 However, Brash-
ear and Phillips12 found a marked
lowering of serum titers of GAD-
like immunoreactivity during
plasmapheresis that correlated
with clinical improvement in one
patient. Corticosteroids have also
been used and were associated
with improvement in four patients
receiving 100 mg/d of predni-
sone2,34 and two patients receiving
60 mg/d of prednisone.33
Accepted for publication October 1;
1993.
Ramachandiran Cooppan, MD,
referred the patient and Christine Mc-
Nulty provided technical assistance.
Pietro De Camilli, MD, performed the
assay for GAD autoantibodies; George
Eisenbarth, MD, performed the as¬
say for islet cell antibodies; and Al¬
berto Pugliese, MD, performed the HLA
typing.
Reprints not available.
